item.title: 1970: Boog Powell, 35 Homers, Selected AL MVP for Orioles
item.description: Boog Powell, first baseman for the American League and World Series champion Baltimore Orioles, is selected AL MVP. Powell (.297, 35 HR, 114 RBI, and named to his fourth All-Star team) beats out two future Hall of Famers from the Minnesota Twins, Tony Oliva and Harmon Killebrew. Photo: Baltimore Orioles (Public domain).

item.title: 2025: Giants Hire Bochy as Special Assistant to Operations
item.description: On November 10, 2025, the San Francisco Giants hired Bochy to serve as a special assistant to their baseball operations department. Photo: Michael Marconi (CC BY 2.0).

item.title: 2023: Guardians Hire Albernaz as Bench Coach
item.description: On November 10, 2023, the Cleveland Guardians hired Albernaz to be their bench coach. Photo: Joel Dinda (CC BY 2.0).

item.title: 2023: Free Agents May Sign With Clubs Other Than Former Club
item.description: First Day of free agents may sign contracts with a club other than a former club.

item.title: 2022: McKay Removed From 40-Man Roster, Sent to Triple–A Durham
item.description: On November 10, 2022, McKay was removed from the 40-man roster and sent outright to Triple–A Durham.

item.title: 2022: Clubs Face Deadline for Qualifying Offers to Free Agents
item.description: Deadline for clubs to make qualifying offers to their eligible players who became free agents

item.title: 2020: Lewis and Williams Win AL and NL Rookie of Year
item.description: Kyle Lewis of the Seattle Mariners and Devin Williams of the Milwaukee Brewers Respectively win the AL And NL Rookies of the Year. Photo: PaulHamaker Cropped by 佾珜 (CC BY-SA 4.0).

item.title: 2020: Twins End Red Wings Partnership in Minor League Overhaul
item.description: On November 10, 2020, Twins management disclosed to the Red Wings that they would be discontinuing their partnership as part of the broad changes in the minor league system for the 2021 season and beyond.

item.title: 2014: Showalter and Williams Win Manager of Year Awards
item.description: Buck Showalter of the Baltimore Orioles and Matt Williams of the Washington Nationals earn the American League Manager of the Year Award in the American League and National League, respectively. Photo: Keith Allison from Hanover, MD, USA (CC BY-SA 2.0).

item.title: 2011: Prieto Named Pitching Coach for Vermont Lake Monsters
item.description: On November 10, 2011, Prieto was announced as the pitching coach for the Vermont Lake Monsters, the Athletics' New York–Penn League (Single A, short season) team.

item.title: 2010: Royals Send DeJesus to Athletics for Marks, Mazzaro
item.description: The Kansas City Royals send David DeJesus to the Oakland Athletics for Justin Marks and Vin Mazzaro. Photo: Keith Allison on Flickr (CC BY-SA 2.0).

item.title: 2010: Dave Niehaus, 75, Hall of Fame Mariners Broadcaster
item.description: Dave Niehaus, 75, Hall of Fame broadcaster for the Seattle Mariners since their inception in 1977 to their final game of the 2010 season. Photo: Gina Catarra from Seattle, WA (CC BY-SA 2.0).

item.title: 2009: GMs Fail to Vote on Expanding Instant Replay
item.description: MLB general managers fail to take a vote on expanding instant replay following a postseason filled with blown calls by umpires, according to Jimmie Lee Solomon, executive vice president of baseball operations in the commissioner's office.

item.title: 2004: Johan Santana Wins AL Cy Young With All 28 First-Place Votes
item.description: Johan Santana of the Minnesota Twins won the American League Cy Young Award. Santana got all of the 28 available first-place votes while winning 20 games and struck out 265 batters. Photo: User Lordcolus (Original version) User UCinternational (Crop) (CC BY 2.0).

item.title: 1999: Padres Trade Andy Ashby to Phillies for Loewer, Eaton, Montgomery
item.description: 12 ERA despite missing nearly four months because of a stress fracture in his right humerus, Loewer was traded along with Adam Eaton and Steve Montgomery from the Phillies to the Padres for Andy Ashby on November 10, 1999.

item.title: 1998: Hal Newhouser, 77, Hall of Fame Tigers Pitcher
item.description: Hal Newhouser, 77, Hall of Fame pitcher for the Detroit Tigers who won back-to-back MVP awards in 1944 and 1945, while topping the American League in wins four times as well as in ERA and strikeouts twice each, and leading Detroit to Game 7 victory over the Chicago Cubs in the 1945 World Series. Photo: Unknown author (Public domain).

item.title: 1993: Frank Thomas Unanimously Named American League MVP
item.description: Chicago White Sox slugger Frank Thomas was unanimously named the American League MVP. The first baseman, who ranks in the top 10 of the league's nine offensive categories, batted .317 with 41 home runs and knocked in 128 RBIs for the divisional champion White Sox. Photo: clare_and_ben User:Delaywaves (CC BY-SA 2.0).

item.title: 1992: Chuck Connors, 71, 1951 Cubs First Baseman, Rifleman Actor
item.description: Chuck Connors, 71, first baseman for the 1951 Chicago Cubs who gained stardom as an actor on the television series The Rifleman. Photo: Photo Associates (Public domain).

item.title: 1992: NL Blocks Giants Sale to Vince Naimoli, 9-4 Vote Falls Short
item.description: The National League fails to approve the sale of the San Francisco Giants to Vince Naimoli, blocking a move to St. Petersburg, Florida. The 9–4 vote falls short of the 10 required for approval.

item.title: 1990: Aurelio Monteagudo, 46, Cuban Pitcher
item.description: Aurelio Monteagudo, 46, Cuban pitcher with five teams who also gained renown for pitching in the Venezuelan and Mexican leagues.

item.title: 1987: Steve Bedrosian Edges Sutcliffe, Reuschel for Closest Cy Young Vote
item.description: In the closest vote in Cy Young Award history, Steve Bedrosian (nine of 24 first-place votes, 57 points) of the Philadelphia Phillies edges Rick Sutcliffe (Chicago Cubs; four first-place votes, 55 points) and Rick Reuschel (San Francisco Giants; eight first-place votes, 54 points) to win National League honors.

item.title: 1987: Bubby Sadler, 78, Negro Leagues Shortstop
item.description: Bubby Sadler, 78, shortstop who played in Negro leagues and with Black barnstorming teams between 1934 and 1944; inducted in 1999 to Delaware Sports Museum and Hall of Fame.

item.title: 1982: Forty Players, Including Don Baylor and Steve Garvey, Granted Free Agency
item.description: Forty players—including veteran standouts Don Baylor (1979 AL MVP) and Steve Garvey (1974 NL MVP)—are granted free agency and will enter the market for new contracts. Photo: Wikimedia Commons (CC BY 2.0).

item.title: 1978: Yankees Send Sparky Lyle to Rangers in Ten-Player Trade
item.description: In a ten-player transaction, the New York Yankees send former Cy Young Award winner Sparky Lyle along with Mike Heath, Larry McCall, Dave Rajsich, Domingo Ramos and cash consideration to the Texas Rangers, in exchange for Juan Beníquez, Mike Griffin, Paul Mirabella, Dave Righetti and minor-leaguer Greg Jemison. Photo: New York Yankees / MLB (Public domain).

item.title: 1976: Jim Palmer Wins Third AL Cy Young Award, First AL Pitcher to Do So
item.description: Jim Palmer of the Baltimore Orioles is named the 1976 American League Cy Young Award winner, becoming the first AL pitcher to win the honor three times. Photo: Unknown (Associated Press) (Public domain).

item.title: 1975: Royals Release Harmon Killebrew, Ending 22-Year Career
item.description: The Kansas City Royals release slugger Harmon Killebrew, ending a 22-year career marked by 573 home runs, good for fifth place on the all-time list. Photo: Unknown author (Public domain).

item.title: 1968: U.S. Beats Cuba to Win Mexico City Tournament
item.description: The Mexico City tournament concludes, with the U.S. team, managed by Mic high State coach Danny Litwhiler, defeating Cuba to win the championship.

item.title: 1965: Willie Mays Named 1965 NL MVP, Edging Koufax and Wills
item.description: San Francisco Giants outfielder Willie Mays, who hit .312 with 52 home runs and 112 RBI, is named 1965 National League MVP. Mays (nine first-place votes, 224 points) edges two Los Angeles Dodgers: Sandy Koufax (six, 177) and Maury Wills (five, 164). Photo: Unknown author (Public domain).

item.title: 1964: Braves Sign 25-Year Lease for New Stadium, Draw 911,951 Fans
item.description: The Milwaukee Braves sign a 25-year lease to play in the new Atlanta–Fulton County Stadium. The Braves' move has been rumored since 1963; this past season, they attracted 911,951 fans, sixth among the NL's ten teams. Photo: Don Ceppi/Scenic South Card Co. (Public domain).

item.title: 1953: Giants End Japan Tour, Each Player Receives Just $331
item.description: The New York Giants end their tour of Japan. It is reported that each Giants player received just $331 of the $3,000 they were promised.

item.title: 1951: Joe DiMaggio Homers, Dom Triples in American All-Star Win in Tokyo
item.description: In Tokyo, 50,000 fans are on hand as an American All-Star team battles a Japanese Central League All-Star team. Joe DiMaggio hits a 400-foot home run in the eighth inning to tie the game at 1–1, then his younger brother Dom laces an RBI-triple in the ninth and later scores to give the Americans a 3–2 victory. The Americans have won 12 games and tied one. Photo: Tom Sande (Public domain).

item.title: 1950: Indians Replace Lou Boudreau With Al López as Manager
item.description: The Cleveland Indians change managers, replacing playing skipper Lou Boudreau with former catcher Al López, 42, who had been managing Triple-A Indianapolis. Boudreau, 33, had led Cleveland to a 728–649–12 (.529) record over nine full seasons, including the 1948 AL pennant and World Series championship. Eleven days later, the future Hall-of-Fame shortstop is unconditionally released at his own request. Photo: RF (Public domain).

item.title: 1948: White Sox Acquire Billy Pierce From Tigers for Aaron Robinson
item.description: In a move that will give them their pitching ace for the next decade, the Chicago White Sox acquire left hander Billy Pierce from the Detroit Tigers in exchange for former All-Star catcher Aaron Robinson. Detroit sweetens the deal by adding $10,000 in cash. Photo: ChicagoEric (CC BY-SA 4.0).

item.title: 1932: Donie Bush Named to Manage Cincinnati Reds Next Year
item.description: Donie Bush, who managed the Minneapolis Millers to the American Association this past season, is named to manage the Cincinnati Reds the next year. Photo: Bain News Service (Public domain).

item.title: 1930: Hippo Vaughn Reinstated by Judge Landis After Eight Years
item.description: Veteran pitcher Hippo Vaughn is reinstated by Judge Landis after eight years of ineligibility. Vaughn, who had lost a double no-hitter duel to Fred Toney in the 1917 season, had jumped the Chicago Cubs in 1922. Vaughn chose to pitch for a semi-professional team following a salary dispute with Chicago. He will go to spring training with the Cubs in 1931 but will fail to make the team at age 43. Photo: Bain News Service, publisher (Public domain).

item.title: 1911: Clark Griffith Buys Controlling Interest in Washington Senators
item.description: Clark Griffith becomes a club owner and president when he joins Philadelphia grain broker William Richardson in buying controlling interest in the Washington Senators for $175,000. Griffith, unable to get financial help from the American League, mortgages his ranch in Montana to raise funds. Photo: National Photo Company Collection (Public domain).

item.title: 1888: New Detroit Club Organized to Replace Disbanded Wolverines
item.description: A new club is organized in Detroit to compete in the International Association during the next season, in order to take the place of the disbanded Detroit Wolverines, who finished in fifth place in the National League this past season. Photo: Hastings, George H., fl. 1885-1896, photographer. (Public domain).

item.title: 1878: Athletics Beat Californias Before 8,000 at Trotting Park
item.description: In the Pacific Coast championship game in California, the Athletics defeat the Californias in front of 8,000 fans at the San Francisco National Trotting Park.
